'''Kenneth James Le Couteur''' (16 September 1920 – 18 April 2011) was a British [[physicist]] who was the foundation Professor of Theoretical Physics at the [[Australian National University]] in [[Canberra]]. During [[World War II]] he worked at [[Bletchley Park]] as a [[cryptanalysis|codebreaker]].

==Early life==
Kenneth James Le Couteur was born in [[Saint Helier]] on the island of [[Jersey]], the son of Philippe Le Couteur, the owner of a carpentry business, and his wife Eva {{nee}} Gartrell. He was educated at Victoria College Preparatory School and [[Victoria College, Jersey|Victoria College]] on Jersey, where he was inspired to become a mathematician by his maths teacher, who had been a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] in England. He received a scholarship to study at [[St John's College, Cambridge]], which he entered in 1938. There he studied mathematics, tutored by [[Ebenezer Cunningham]], who had been the senior wrangler in 1902,<ref name="HR">{{cite journal |url=https://www.science.org.au/files/userfiles/fellowship/memoirs/documents/kenneth-james-le-couteur-hr.pdf |journal=Historical Records of Australian Science |year=2012 |volume=23 |pages=176–186 |doi=10.1071/HR12012 |title=Kenneth James Le Couteur 1920–2011 |first=B. A. |last=Robson |issue=2 |access-date=17 October 2016 }}</ref> and rowed for the college.<ref name="SMH">{{cite news |newspaper=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |url=http://www.smh.com.au/comment/obituaries/top-physicist-played-key-wartime-role-20110605-1fnds.html |title=Top physicist played key wartime role |date=6 June 2011 |first=Rodney |last=Baxter |access-date=17 October 2016 }}</ref>

The [[German occupation of the Channel Islands]] in 1940 left him stranded in England, cut off from his family. He was awarded his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1941, winning the [[Mayhew Prize]] for the student showing the greatest distinction in applied mathematics.<ref name="HR" /> He was recruited by the [[Government Code and Cypher School]] at [[Bletchley Park]] as a [[cryptanalyst]]. Le Couteur worked on the [[Enigma machine]]s, and then the [[Lorenz cipher]], codenamed ''Tunny'' by the British. The codebreaking process was partly automated, using [[Heath Robinson (codebreaking machine)|Robinson machines]] and the [[Colossus computer]]s.<ref name="HR"/><ref name="SMH"/>

After the war ended in 1945, Le Couteur returned to Cambridge as a Fellow of St John's College, where he worked on his doctorate. His academic supervisor initially was  [[Maurice Pryce]], but he became the [[Wykeham Professor]] of Physics at [[Oxford University]] in 1946, and [[Nicholas Kemmer]] took over. Le Couteur was awarded a Turner and Newall Fellowship to study at the [[University of Manchester]], where he completed his doctorate in 1948–49 under the supervision of [[Léon Rosenfeld]]. His thesis, on Meson Theory, was submitted in 1949, and he was awarded his [[PhD]] from Cambridge. At Manchester, he began investigation of the evaporation theory of [[decay chain|nuclear disintegration]]. He also met Enid Margaret Domville, who worked there as a librarian. They were married on 14 July 1950.<ref name="HR"/> They had three children, all daughters: [[Caroline Le Couteur|Caroline]], Penelope and Mary (Avinashi), and a foster daughter, Marion Chesher.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://physics.anu.edu.au/theophys/news.php?NewsID=22 |title=Foundation Professor Kenneth Le Couteur has passed away aged 90 |publisher=[[Australian National University]] |access-date=17 October 2016 }}</ref>

==Academic career==
Le Couteur became a lecturer in physics at the [[University of Liverpool]] in 1949. There he continued developing [[relativistic wave equations]] and working on his evaporation theory. He also provided theoretical physicist support of the work of the experimentalists working on the university's 37-inch [[cyclotron]], and collaborated with [[Ernest Titterton]] from the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] (AERE) in [[Harwell, Oxfordshire]]. His work on the Peeler-Regenerative Beam Extraction Method brought him renown, and his solution was employed in the design of subsequent cyclotrons. He also became known for his work on the statistical model of excited nuclei, which he would continue to pursue in Australia.<ref name="HR"/>

In 1956, [[Mark Oliphant]] recruited Le Couteur as the foundation Professor of Theoretical Physics at the [[Australian National University]] in [[Canberra]]. When Le Couteur arrived, the faculty of the department consisted of himself and Frederick Barker. He enjoyed the new location, sailing and rock fishing on the nearby [[South Coast (New South Wales)|South Coast of New South Wales]], and sailing on [[Lake Burley Griffin]] after the lake was filled in 1964. Le Couteur took up the position in April 1956, and remained there for the rest of his career,<ref name="HR"/> except for study leave at [[CERN]]<ref>{{Cite report|last=Le Couteur|first=Kenneth|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/931879|title=Construction of a non relativistic s-matrix from its poles|publisher=CERN|year=1959|location=Geneva|docket=CERN-TH-64}}</ref> and the AERE in 1959 and 1960.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://physics.anu.edu.au/theophys/history.php |title=History – Theoretical Physics – ANU |publisher=[[Australian National University]] |access-date=17 October 2016 }}</ref> In 1960 he was elected as a Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science. He was the acting Director of the Research School of Physical Sciences on many occasions, occupying the position for extended periods from September 1973 until September 1974, and from February to December 1978.<ref name="HR"/>

In 1962 Le Couteur arranged for the department to acquire an [[IBM 1620]] as its first computer; it was programmed for numerical calculations in the [[FORTRAN]] language. He was also involved in the design and planning of a new Mathematical Sciences building, completed in 1963 and in 1996 renamed the Le Couteur Building.<ref name="HR"/> He was recognised with the award of the [[Centenary Medal]] in 2001 "for service to Australian society and science in theoretical physics".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dpmc.gov.au/government/its-honour/search-australian-honours |title=Le Couteur, Kenneth James |publisher=Australian Government |access-date=17 October 2016 |archive-date=6 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170506130853/http://www.dpmc.gov.au/government/its-honour/search-australian-honours |url-status=dead }}</ref>  When he retired in December 1985, he became a [[professor emeritus]], which he remained until 1989.<ref name="HR"/>

In 1988, he moved to the Ginninderra Gardens Aged Care Facility in the Canberra suburb of [[Page, Australian Capital Territory|Page]]. He died on 18 April 2011. He was survived by his wife and daughters.<ref name="SMH"/>
